Franz Schubert. The Austrian composer who bridged the late Classical and early Romantic eras, despite dying at only thirty-one years old.

Despite his short life, Schubert was exceptionally prolific. He composed over six hundred vocal art songs, known as Lieder, nine symphonies, and a vast body of chamber and piano music. His music is marked by its gift for melody and expressive harmony, establishing German song as a major classical genre.

He revolutionized the Lieder genre by composing over six hundred pieces. Among the most famous are settings of Goethe's poems like Erlkönig, depicting a father and child chased by the supernatural Erlking, and Gretchen am Spinnrade, which imitates a spinning wheel in the piano accompaniment.

His Symphony No. 8 in B minor is universally known as the Unfinished Symphony because it consists of only two completed movements rather than the traditional four.

The Trout Quintet, his Piano Quintet in A major, is a popular chamber work named because its fourth movement is a set of variations on his own Lied Die Forelle, meaning The Trout. It is scored for piano, violin, viola, cello, and double bass.

His String Quartet No. 14 in D minor is called Death and the Maiden, a dramatic chamber masterpiece named for its second movement, which is a set of variations on his Lied Der Tod und das Mädchen.

Winterreise, or Winter Journey, is his celebrated late song cycle of twenty-four poems by Wilhelm Müller. It charts a rejected lover's lonely, winter wanderings.

Living in Vienna in the shadow of Beethoven, Schubert struggled for financial success. He was chiefly celebrated in private gatherings called Schubertiades before achieving posthumous fame. He was a torchbearer at Beethoven's funeral and requested to be buried next to him, which he was. His Lieder applied dramatic, character-driven storytelling to song form.
